The revelations have raised questions about Nvidia’s corporate oversight and its business dealings involving Beijing. The committee will also retain independent outside experts to provide legal, national security and trade compliance expertise. President Donald Trump welcomed the announcement Tuesday, saying it was a good idea for Nvidia to launch a national security initiative. queue.title: Little-known IRS program could be unfairly crushing landowners, according to alarming study and whistleblower
queue.dek: An Infinity Advisory Services study found the IRS slashed conservation easement values by an average of roughly 97% across 115 cases examined.
queue.opening: FIRST ON FOX: A new study is raising questions about whether the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) has been putting its finger on the scale to hit American landowners with higher tax bills through a little-known conservation tax program, as a whistleblower who spent many years at the agency warns the findings show the IRS has "lost its way." The study, conducted by Infinity Advisory Services, examined more than 130 IRS valuation reviews and found that, in 115 conservation easement tax incentive cases with comparable figures, the agency slashed taxpayers’ appraised values by an average of roughly 97%, with reductions of 99% or more common. The study makes the case that the pattern across different properties, tax years and reviewers points to a process designed to reach a predetermined answer, which effectively wiped out the value underpinning taxpayers’ conservation deductions rather than fairly evaluating each property. The conservation easement tax incentive allows landowners to claim a charitable tax deduction for permanently giving up certain development rights on their property, helping preserve farmland , forests and other protected land. The landowners keep ownership, but restrictions limit how the property can be developed. An appraisal determines the value of the rights donated, which generally forms the basis of the deduction and is at the center of these IRS disputes. queue.title: Pizza Hut co-founder Dan Carney, who turned $600 loan from mom into global restaurant empire, dead at 95
queue.dek: Dan Carney borrowed $600 from his mother to open the first Pizza Hut with his brother Frank in Wichita, Kansas, in 1958, then sold the global chain to PepsiCo for $300 million.
queue.opening: Dan Carney, who borrowed $600 from his mother to open a small Kansas pizza restaurant with his younger brother and turned it into the global Pizza Hut empire , has died. He was 95. Carney was just 26 when he and his younger brother, Frank, opened their first Pizza Hut in Wichita in 1958, using money borrowed from their mother. The brothers began franchising the business a year later, expanded internationally in 1970 and sold the chain to PepsiCo for $300 million in 1977, according to Wichita State University. Carney died Friday, Nov. 13, surrounded by his family, according to an obituary published by Cozine Memorial Group. A cause of death was not specified. AMERICA'S BEST-TASTING PIZZA CHAIN IS AN OLD-SCHOOL FAVORITE, SURVEY FINDS Born Oct. 6, 1931, in Kansas City, Missouri , Carney grew up in Wichita as one of 12 siblings. He graduated from Wichita University with a degree in business and economics and later earned an MBA from Wichita State University. He also served as a first lieutenant in the U.S. Air Force. The brothers' restaurant began in a small building at the corner of Bluff and Kellogg in Wichita, at a time when pizza was still relatively unfamiliar to many American diners. What started as a gamble on an emerging food trend quickly grew into a pioneering franchise operation. queue.dek: California's Bay Area bridge tolls will climb to $9 for FasTrak users and $10 for mailed invoices starting Jan. 1, 2027, as seven state-owned bridges face rate hikes.
queue.opening: Drivers in one of the biggest states in the nation are venting over a new round of bridge toll increases that could soon cost some drivers $10 per crossing — and have a spillover impact on millions of others who never even cross the bridges. Starting Jan. 1, 2027, new rates will take effect on seven state-owned bridges in California's San Francisco Bay Area , according to an alert from Bay Area FasTrak. Drivers using a FasTrak toll tag will pay $9 for a standard two-axle vehicle, while those with a registered license plate account will pay $9.25. Drivers who receive an invoice in the mail will pay $10, the alert said. MAJOR US VACATION DESTINATION COULD GET MORE EXPENSIVE AS OFFICIALS EYE NEW FEES The changes will affect the San Francisco-Oakland Bay, Antioch, Benicia-Martinez, Carquinez, Dumbarton, Richmond-San Rafael and San Mateo-Hayward bridges. (The Golden Gate Bridge is not included.) The Bay Area Toll Authority (BATA) told Fox News Digital the increases are needed to maintain, repair and operate the bridges as they age. "State law requires the Bay Area Toll Authority — working in partnership with Caltrans [California's Department of Transportation] — to keep the state-owned toll bridges structurally sound and in good repair," BATA said in a statement. "These bridges range in age from 13 to 90 years old, and maintenance and rehab costs increase as the bridges age." queue.dek: Iran's IRGC claims it struck a U.S. radar system at the Sheikh Isa base in Bahrain, home to the Fifth Fleet, the third attack in five days after a lull.
queue.opening: Iran fired drones toward what it said was a U.S. military radar system in Bahrain on Tuesday, marking the third strike in five days after a roughly two-month lull in the conflict, Reuters reported. Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said its target was the radar system at the Sheikh Isa base in Bahrain, which is home to the U.S. Fifth Fleet . Bahrain said its air defenses intercepted the incoming drones after authorities issued a security alert urging residents to seek shelter. Officials announced an all-clear later in the morning, with no deaths or injuries reported. U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) also addressed the Iranian drone strikes, saying they didn't hit their intended target. The drones were "intercepted without any damage to U.S. equipment or injury to American personnel," CENTCOM said. IRAN’S DRONE HUNT ESCALATES AS TEHRAN TARGETS US SPY TECH TO EXPOSE BATTLEFIELD SECRETS The attempted attack followed another wave of Iranian aerial strikes that Bahrain repelled on Sunday, when the IRGC claimed six of its drones targeted a radar system at the Al-Riffa helicopter base. That strike came two days after Friday's initial attempt against a U.S. radar installation in Bahrain — the first major attack after the two-month pause. U.S. Central Command said American forces shot down both drones in that incident, with no casualties or injuries. queue.title: ‘Frightened’ Texas neighbors left to wonder what political domino will fall next
queue.dek: Oklahoma, Arkansas and Louisiana residents react to Texas flipping blue in the 2026 midterm election, fearing a chain reaction could reach red states.
queue.opening: After the blue wave hit Texas in the 2026 midterm election, residents of neighboring red states are wondering whether their state could be next. Fox News Digital traveled to Oklahoma, Arkansas and Louisiana to ask residents how they view the political shift in Texas and whether they think their state could flip in the near future. Residents in these states said the economy and protecting conservative values were among their top issues. TED CRUZ SAYS 'BLUE TSUNAMI' TOOK OVER TEXAS AFTER DEMOCRATS SWEPT STATEWIDE RACES Residents in the small town of Guthrie, Oklahoma, during a morning breakfast stop at Katie’s Diner, expressed concern about their southern neighbor electing Democrats, and believe that if it can happen in Texas, it can happen in the Sooner State. Roger from Guthrie said, "It's awful, isn't it? I blame it a lot on the Democrats when they let all those people cross the border." Stephanie from Guthrie shared the feeling and said she never saw it coming. "I'm a little frightened by it, to be perfectly honest," she said. "The values that were so close, Texas values, were so close to Oklahoma values, and more of a Christian state. And I hope that's still the case there." Curtis from Guthrie said, "All I can do is pray for them, because … I felt like they were deceived and lied to about some of the things that their politicians were talking about, and they're going to find out that they were." Curtis added that Oklahoma could be next if people stay home and don't vote.

queue.title: Clarence Thomas calls foul on California ruling he says could turn citizens into government mouthpieces
queue.dek: Clarence Thomas warns the Supreme Court's refusal to hear a California implicit bias case leaves states free to compel speech from private citizens.
queue.opening: Justice Clarence Thomas warned Monday that the Supreme Court is leaving the door open for states to compel speech from private citizens by not taking up a challenge to a California law. On Monday, the Supreme Court declined a petition to hear a case from a California physician who argued that the state government was forcing her to make statements she disagreed with while teaching a mandatory course for doctors. Thomas was joined by Justice Samuel Alito in dissenting from the decision, arguing that allowing the law to stand could have implications reaching far beyond the medical field. The case stems from California’s requirement that all its licensed physicians complete 50 hours of state-approved continuing education courses every two years. California requires continuing medical education courses to include instruction on implicit bias, either through examples of how it affects physicians' treatment decisions and health outcomes or strategies for addressing how those biases may contribute to healthcare disparities. "When, as here, the government does not issue its own messages but instead requires private speakers to communicate the government’s viewpoint, the First Amendment applies," Thomas wrote. "A State cannot regulate its way out of First Amendment scrutiny. We should not permit the government-speech doctrine to be wielded as ‘a cover for censorship’ or a cloak for compelled speech." queue.opening: It’s Monday, November 16. This is The Front Page , your daily window into the world of The Free Press —and our take on the world at large. Today: Eli Lake on the Democrats’ showdown over who will lead the Senate. Jed Rubenfeld on the strange case of Ilhan Omar. Coleman Hughes interviews Ben Shapiro. And much more. But first: How much is one CEO worth? On Sunday, the Financial Times reported that Jensen Huang and his allies were plotting his return as CEO of Nvidia, the giant chip maker he co-founded and ran until his resignation last week. On one level, the idea is—how to put this?—insane. Only last week, Huang stepped down after reports of three affairs—one with an alleged Chinese spy and two with women who reported to him at Nvidia—and is now being scrutinized (including by Matt Pottinger and Liza Tobin in these pages ) over allegations he worked to evade export controls on chips. How could Huang possibly do the job again? But consider a number: $570 billion. That’s how much Nvidia’s stock market value has dropped since the start of the scandal. It’s therefore arguably a crude measure of Huang’s value to the company. And, when faced with that many zeros, what are a few indiscretions? Or so the members of Nvidia’s board of directors might be asking themselves. queue.opening: A coordinated social media operation aimed at influencing voters ahead of the midterm elections was led in part by an 80-year-old socialist organizer who spent decades helping build the modern left's activist infrastructure, according to tax records reviewed by Fox News Digital. "The Republicans never figured out what we were doing," political commentator Van Jones said earlier this month on CNN's "The Source" with Kaitlan Collins. "There’s something called the American Accountability Network: tens of thousands of online humans, not bots, coordinated to make the affordability message a winning message online … Don’t get mad at me. I was given permission to reveal this." The American Accountability Network (AAN), which incorporation documents show was founded in early 2025, is an online activist organization that recruited both large content creators, as well as everyday Americans, and tasked them with posting, sharing and otherwise amplifying rhetoric that framed Democrats as the party of affordability — a message that exit polls suggest resonated with the electorate. Tax documents identify the woman behind the effort as Heather Booth, AAN’s president and an 80-year-old self-described "socialist feminist" who has been deeply involved in far-left activism since the anti-war movement of the Vietnam era. queue.dek: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy expects flights to normalize Monday after an FAA communications outage caused widespread cancellations and delays nationwide.
queue.opening: Air travel across the U.S. faces a key test Monday as airlines work to resume normal operations following a nationwide ground stop that disrupted thousands of flights, while federal officials investigate router problems at two facilities as a possible cause of the communications failure. As of 7 a.m. ET Monday, 284 flights within, into or out of the United States had been canceled and another 954 delayed, according to flight-tracking website FlightAware. American Airlines led carriers with 157 cancellations, followed by SkyWest with 41 and JetBlue with 30. The disruptions followed a weekend of widespread flight problems. By early Monday, more than 28,300 flights had been delayed and 18,520 canceled since Friday, underscoring the scale of the travel turmoil.
